chapter_theme: Civakan's friends gather to free him from the usurper's prison by Padumukan's plan, and Gandharvadattai, able to free him by her spells, holds back because a husband saved by his wife would be shamed; Civakan too refuses her magic and calls on his friend, the god once a dog, who comes down in a storm and carries him off, while Madanan's men kill a stranger in his place and Kattiyangaran rewards the supposed murder.

cast.role: the hero, held prisoner by the usurper
Civakan's friend, author of the rescue plan, called தாமரை நாமன் in 1145
one of Civakan's companions, brother of Nabulan
Civakan's younger brother, called நந்தன் in 1144
Gunamalai's father, who joins the rescue with his sons
Civakan's Vidyadhara wife, mistress of spells
the armed powers of Gandharvadattai's spell-lore, called விண்ணோர் and எந்தைமார் in 1160
the god, once the dog Civakan gave the mantra to, who carries him out of captivity
Kattiyangaran's brother-in-law, sent to execute Civakan

1142.reading: The plan goes on: when Madanan, who escorts the prisoner, comes down the street, the speaker will lay his head on the ground with a crescent-headed arrow, and as the warriors scatter in confusion the others are to take the young man and go into a thicket that even men of war cannot enter.
1142.nuance: The speaker is not named here; 1145 calls the plan the policy told by the man named for the lotus (தாமரை நாமன்), Padumukan, so these two verses are read as his.

1143.reading: If the enemy fight there, they are to send them swiftly to the other world with their swords, and he will hurry after them; he bids them make firm at once the friendship that the whole world has proved, he who was like the death of all the deaths gathered together.
1143.nuance: Line 3 (மாற்றிய நட்பு வல்லே வலிப்புறீஇ) is hard to construe; the reading takes it as a charge to hold fast to their friendship in the fight.

1144.reading: Like diseases round Death, Nabulan and Vipulan close round; Nandattan appears with his spear so that all fear him, and Gunamalai's father, his sons and others of their side gather and stand round like a pack of leaping tigers.
1144.event: Civakan's companions, his brother and Gunamalai's father and kin gather under arms for the rescue.
1144.nuance: The bride's father joins his son-in-law's friends against the usurper: the new marriage has already made a kin party in the city.

1145.reading: While these stand on guard according to the plan Padumukan told, Gandharvadattai, of the silk-draped waist and coral mouth, hears of what has happened.

1146.reading: She takes an auspicious cloth from a gem-set Yavana casket and puts it on, sets fragrant garlands from a gold casket and a costly necklace on herself, and begins the rite for the trouble that has come upon her husband.
1146.event: Gandharvadattai dresses in auspicious cloth and ornaments to begin a rite for her husband.

1147.reading: Anointing herself with white paste and water from a gold vessel set with gems, the tender one recites all her spells, and the powers of her lore, bearing sword and spear, stone, fire and wind, come and surround the divine woman.
1147.event: Gandharvadattai recites her Vidyadhara spells and their armed powers gather round her.
1147.nuance: The princess of the Vidyadharas commands a war magic of her own: the rescue that the men are planning with arrows she could do alone, which is what the next verses weigh.

1148.reading: She of the bamboo shoulders stands thinking that she could take away the hero's pain as fast as lightning, gently, and waits for the moment, and then she reflects that a lasting blame on earth would come of it to the noble one.
1148.event: Gandharvadattai, ready to free Civakan by magic, hesitates for fear of the blame it would bring him.

1149.reading: She asks the god what she is to do: if, while he is sunk in the king's prison as in the great sea, his wife comes to him and frees him, what then are his strength and learning worth, and how is the blame to be borne that would sweep the world for nothing?

claims.claim: a man freed from danger by his wife loses the credit of his own strength and learning

1149.nuance: The shame of a man rescued by a woman is voiced by the woman who could rescue him, and it holds her hand: the epic lets the wife carry the husband's honour code.

1150.reading: She goes on: if it is said that Fortune herself freed the lord from prison there is no blame, as if there were no difference between Fortune and herself; but Fortune of the lotus is a woman common to all, while she, of the silver mountain, is a wife of family.

claims.claim: Fortune is a woman common to all, unlike a wife of good family who belongs to one man

1150.nuance: The word division of lines 1-3 is doubtful; the reading takes செய்யவள் as the goddess of fortune and வெள்ளிம்மலை as Gandharvadattai's Vidyadhara home set against the lotus. On that reading she refuses the cover story that his luck saved him, because the help of a wife, unlike the help of fortune, would be his shame.

1151.reading: Saying 'let what must be, be; fame and blame last but seven days, and I will not seek them out among gods or men; ache, my heart', the peacock-gentle one stands gazing toward the prisoner like a cow newly calved toward her calf in the pen.
1151.event: Gandharvadattai holds back her magic and stands watching over Civakan in his captivity.
1151.nuance: Line 1 (புகழும் புழியும் மெழு நாளவை) is read as fame and blame lasting seven days, which would be her setting reputation aside; the line is garbled as divided and the sense is not sure.

1152.reading: Civakan ponders: burning the great city is one course, destroying Madanan another, and the plan of his matchless friends may stand, but he does not want to go on living set free by the spells of his bamboo-shouldered wife.
1152.event: Civakan, bound, rejects rescue by his wife's magic.

claims.claim: it is better not to live than to live freed by one's wife's power

1152.nuance: The husband reaches the same refusal as the wife (1149) without hearing her: both hold that his life is worth less than his name if she saves him.

1153.reading: He says he will tear through the massed elephants as a must elephant loosed on men splits them, or as a raging lion leaps into a flock of goats, seizing crown and flank and drinking their lives.
1153.nuance: குச்சென நிரைத்த (line 4) is obscure; the elephants are taken as ranked close like a thicket.

1154.reading: Striking elephant with elephant and chariot with chariot till hot blood surges, he could drink the life of that man, but the day of his end has not come; if this worm should kill him, he says, he will think of his friend.
1154.event: Civakan resolves to call on his friend the god if the usurper moves to kill him.
1154.nuance: இக்கிருமி, 'this worm', is Civakan's word for the usurper. எல்லைநாள் வந்ததில்லை makes the timing of the enemy's death a set limit, not his own choice; the 'friend' is the god who was the dog of the bathing festival.

1155.reading: His friend the god sat among his goddesses beside a celestial dancer, shining on his chest like a young crescent on the sun rising from the sea, listening to them sing Civakan's virtues to the yazh.
1155.event: Sudanjanan, in his heaven, listens to his goddesses sing Civakan's virtues.
1155.nuance: The heaven he enjoys is the one his friend's mantra won him (947), and what its women sing there is the friend's praise.

1156.reading: The bright god with the diamond crown felt his left lotus eye throb, thought of the one dear to him as life, saw what had befallen him by his far-seeing knowledge, and leaving a likeness for his peacock-like goddesses rose through the great sky.
1156.event: Warned by an omen, Sudanjanan learns of Civakan's peril and sets out from heaven.
1156.nuance: ஓதி is read as the gods' far-seeing knowledge (avadhi); மயிலனார்க்குப் படி வைத்து is read as leaving a likeness or token for his consorts, which is doubtful. The throbbing eye works as an omen on a god as on a mortal.

1157.reading: Thunder, lightning and roaring filled the world as if the wind of the aeon's end were tearing out the mountains; the sun hid as though ashamed to see the distress, and rain poured down as if the sea had been lifted and thrown upon the land.
1157.event: A storm and darkness fall on the city as the god comes down.

1158.reading: With sky and earth indistinguishable, beasts and men robbed of sight and speech, and women and men crying 'see, the sea has taken it', the lord lifted the king's son Civakan, held him to his breast, and rose and went.
1158.event: Under cover of the storm, Sudanjanan lifts Civakan and carries him away through the sky.

1159.reading: As he rose carrying the hill-shouldered one, she of the fair brow blessed him, 'may good come', and with that blessing one thought rose in her: when will be the day her eyes see again the youth for whom her heart aches?
1159.event: Gandharvadattai blesses the departing rescuer and longs to see Civakan again.

1160.reading: In the fragrant ground strewn with garlands she praised the heavenly ones who had come, scattered flowers, and sent them away, saying 'my fathers, rise', she whose voice outdoes the parrot's.
1160.event: Gandharvadattai dismisses with worship the spell-powers she had summoned.
1160.nuance: The powers called up in 1147 go back unused: her restraint, not her magic, is what the episode records of her.

1161.reading: Madanan, brother-in-law of the king of many elephants, who had brought the spear-bearing youth out to kill him, cannot find the handsome one; sighing and staring in fear, he speaks to the bowmen.
1161.event: Madanan finds Civakan gone and turns in fear to his men.
1161.nuance: Madanan is the king's மைத்துனன் here, which ties the executioner to the usurper by marriage.

1162.reading: He says they came to kill the youth the king raged at, and asks what they will now say and do, for if it is known what has happened the king will burn them like lamp wicks; let them gather round and tell him what to do.
1162.nuance: எரிவிளக் குறுக்கு நம்மை is read as the king burning them like lamps; the phrase is hard as divided. The fear of the tyrant, not loyalty, drives what follows.

1163.reading: Seeking a way to save their lives, the plotters agreed, seized one man, split him with a sword and rolled his body over, and the fair city grieved like people on a sinking ship.
1163.event: Madanan's men kill a bystander and pass his corpse off as Civakan's, and the city mourns.

1164.reading: Madanan tells the king: the youth who fought the elephant, with a great crowd thronging and rain, darkness and wind making escape likely, was in fear of losing him split open in the chest and rolled over.
1164.event: Madanan falsely reports to Kattiyangaran that Civakan has been killed.
1164.nuance: The lie is built on the true storm: the god's darkness becomes the executioner's excuse.

1165.reading: The king says no one in the world has Civakan's nature, his grace, strength, manliness, learning, beauty, wisdom, youth, zeal, giving, enjoyment, firm fame and kin, that it was very hard to kill such a man, and honours Madanan with a reward.
1165.event: Kattiyangaran praises the supposedly dead Civakan and rewards Madanan for killing him.
1165.nuance: The usurper lists the very virtues that make Civakan fit to rule and rewards his murder for that reason: the praise is the measure of the threat.

links.note: The patikam tells that a god came down the sky's path like lightning from a cloud and carried the strong one away from the king's prison; here Sudanjanan feels the omen, learns the danger and descends in storm.
links.teaches: The patikam's single line is filled out with the god's heaven, his omen and his far-seeing knowledge, so the rescue is shown as the answer of a bond, not a stroke of luck.

links.note: In 947 Civakan gives the dying dog the five padas and it leaves its body; here the dog, now a god among goddesses, comes down to save the one who gave it the mantra.
links.teaches: Read together, the two scenes make the mantra given out of pity into the cause of the hero's deliverance, the Jain epic's way of showing a good deed returning within the same story.

links.note: Kural 107 says people remember through seven births the friendship of those who wiped away their sorrow; Civakan, facing death, counts on the friend whose death-sorrow he eased in another body.
links.teaches: The epic makes the couplet's seven births literal: a dog that became a god still keeps the debt, and the debtor runs to the man who wiped his tears.

gains.a: a moral frame that makes Civakan's appeal to the god a claim of gratitude rather than a call on magic
gains.b: a case where the remembered friendship crosses an actual rebirth from beast to god, which the couplet only asserts as a span of time

links.note: Kural 903 says stooping before one's wife brings a man shame among the good; Gandharvadattai, able to free Civakan, holds back because being saved by his wife would shame his strength and learning.
links.teaches: The couplet's shame is a man's fear of his wife's power, but here the wife herself fears it on his behalf and keeps her power idle, so the rule's cost falls on the woman who could act.

gains.a: a source in Tamil ethics for the code that stops her hand
gains.b: a scene showing the rule enforced from the woman's side, at the price of leaving the husband in danger

links.note: Kural 967 holds it better to be called ruined than to live following those who scorn one; Civakan says he does not want to live if he is set free by his wife's spells.
links.teaches: The epic turns the couplet's preference for ruin over dishonour onto rescue by a wife, so honour can refuse even a loving help, and the story then lets a male friend's help pass as honourable.

gains.a: a name, maanam, for the choice Civakan makes in chains
gains.b: an instance where the dishonourable life is not servitude to enemies but survival by a woman's power, which shows how gendered the couplet's honour could be made

links.note: Kural 327 forbids taking another's life even to save one's own; Madanan's men, fearing the king, kill a stranger and pass him off as Civakan to save themselves.
links.teaches: The story shows the exact deed the couplet forbids and shows its source in the tyrant's terror, so the rule against killing is seen giving way first where the sceptre is bent.

gains.a: the Kural's measure for judging an act the narration only reports
gains.b: a case of the forbidden trade of life for life driven by fear of a king, which ties the chapter on not killing to the chapter on oppressive rule

links.note: The storm the god raises in 1157 to hide the rescue is the rain, darkness and wind Madanan cites in 1164 as the reason he had Civakan cut down.
links.teaches: The one storm serves two ends: it hides the god's rescue and gives the killers the alibi that lets the usurper believe his rival dead.

links.note: Buddhisenan's plan in 1140 is to burn the city and free Civakan by force; Civakan here sets both that and his wife's magic aside and waits on his friend.
links.teaches: The prisoner overrules all the rescues offered him, so his deliverance comes only from the bond he made himself, which is the episode's point about merit.

new_concepts.gloss: the vidya: the spell-lore of the Vidyadharas, recited to summon powers and weapons
new_concepts.label_source: the verses use விஞ்ஞை (1147) and விஞ்சை (1152)

source_issues: Most verses were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four by the build (FLAG repaired); word division inside joined lines is often doubtful.
1144 line 1 has சூழந்த, apparently for சூழ்ந்த.
1150 lines 1-3 and 1151 line 1 (புகழும் புழியும் மெழு நாளவை) are hard to construe as divided.
1165 line 2 நிண்பு looks like a misprint, perhaps for நண்பு.
